thread.title: Abiodun Highlights Need for 554,000 State Police Officers to Boost Security
thread.title_full: Abiodun Highlights Need for 554,000 State Police Officers to Boost Security

author: LeadershipNGA
title: Abiodun Highlights Need for 554,000 State Police Officers to Boost Security
text:
Ogun State Governor Dapo Abiodun states Nigeria requires an additional 554,353 personnel for State Policing, urging urgent implementation and sustainable financing to decentralize security and address local challenges.
Chairman of the Southern Governors’ Forum and Ogun State Governor, Dapo Abiodun, has disclosed that Nigeria would require an additional 554,353 personnel to adequately staff the proposed He warned that the success of the reform would depend on a sustainable financing arrangement that would not leave poorer states behind.
Abiodun, who made the disclosure on Thursday, while delivering the keynote address at the posthumous 70th birthday colloquium of former Ondo State Governor, the late Oluwarotimi Akeredolu, held at the International Conference Centre, University of Ibadan, said State Police had moved beyond advocacy to a national imperative requiring urgent and practical implementation. The colloquium, organised in honour of Akeredolu under the theme, “Fundamentals and Governance of State Policing: Towards a New Architecture for National Security in Nigeria,” brought together governors, former governors, lawmakers, security chiefs, traditional rulers, academics, civil society actors, family members, friends and professional associates of the late governor.
Abiodun said empirical data from the Nigeria Governors’ Forum showed that, based on the United Nations ratio of one police officer to 414 citizens, the country would need 554,353 additional State Police personnel, which would translate to about 184,784 recruits annually over three years.
“The debate is no longer whether Nigeria needs State Police, but how swiftly and sustainably we establish it,” Abiodun said, insisting that the country could no longer sustain a security architecture in which every policing responsibility was effectively centralised in Abuja. He said the security challenges confronting the country had exposed the limitations of the existing arrangement, stressing that policing must be brought closer to the people.
“Security is intrinsically local. You cannot police a community whose language you do not speak, whose terrain you do not know. State policing is not a threat to unity; it is the bedrock of stability and prosperity,” he said.
The governor, who is also the Chairman of the NGF Committee on State Police and a member of the Presidential Working Group on the National Policing Bill, said the financial realities of the states must, however, be addressed before the new policing structure can take effect. According to him, only five states, Lagos, Rivers, the Federal Capital Territory, Ogun and Enugu, accounted for 61.6 per cent of Internally Generated Revenue, while 76 per cent of the states generated below the national average of N13,600 per capita, with half earning less than N6,334 per capita.
Abiodun warned that such disparities could undermine the proposed reform if the Federal Government and states failed to establish a financing mechanism to guarantee a minimum level of policing capacity across the federation.
“Insecurity in low-revenue states spills over nationally. Underfunding one state’s police becomes everyone’s crisis,” he said. He consequently advocated the establishment of a constitutional State Police Take-Off Fund, built around equal-access grants, need-based top-ups, and standards-linked disbursement, arguing that security must not become a function of the financial strength of the state in which a citizen resides.
The Ogun governor said the Presidential Working Group was already developing operational blueprints, financial models, accountability mechanisms and legislative oversight arrangements for the proposed system, including frameworks for recruitment, training, governance and redress for abuses. He outlined eight fundamentals that must underpin the State Police architecture, including a clear legal framework; professional and merit-based recruitment and training; personnel welfare; predictable and sustainable funding; effective use of technology; safeguards against political abuse; deliberate community engagement; and coordination across state boundaries.
The governor said recruitment must be transparent, properly vetted, and representative, while officers must be trained in investigation, evidence handling, lawful arrest, conflict management, proportionate use of force, and the protection of vulnerable persons. He also insisted that political affiliation must never determine access to police protection, adding, “Political opponents, journalists, peaceful protesters and minority communities deserve equal protection. ” “Disagreement with a government cannot diminish a citizen’s rights. We must earn public confidence through safeguards that work,” he said.
Abiodun further called for adequate welfare for personnel, including regular remuneration, proper equipment, medical care, insurance and dependable support for their families.
“Welfare, discipline and accountability should develop together,” he said, adding that funding arrangements must be transparent and sustainable enough to cover salaries, training, maintenance, communications, investigations and equipment replacement. He warned against allowing private interests to dictate police operations, saying security trust funds could supplement public financing only under clear rules and public accountability.
“Private contributions must follow clear rules and public accountability; they must never purchase influence over investigations or preferential treatment,” he said. The governor also canvassed the use of secure communications, coordinated databases, surveillance and reliable emergency reporting systems to strengthen intelligence gathering and response, but stressed that technology must operate within the law and with safeguards for privacy and accountable access to information.
Abiodun said the proposed system must also prevent the police from becoming an instrument of political repression, insisting on independent complaints mechanisms, legislative scrutiny and judicial remedies. He urged the involvement of traditional rulers, religious leaders, women’s organisations, youth groups, farmers, transport workers and other community stakeholders in building an effective intelligence-gathering system.
The governor said coordination between federal and state security agencies would be critical, particularly because criminals could exploit jurisdictional boundaries if agencies failed to share intelligence and conduct joint operations. Abiodun noted that Amotekun had demonstrated that local intelligence and regional cooperation could complement the Federal Police and provide faster responses to threats.
The governor said Akeredolu’s vision extended beyond security to regional economic development, noting that the late governor also supported the emergence of the Southwest Development Commission as part of the wider effort to build a secure and prosperous region. He said the most fitting tribute to Akeredolu would not be ceremonies but the completion of the reforms he championed.
He commended President Bola Tinubu for supporting State Police reform through an appropriate constitutional framework and urged stakeholders to ensure that the process reached its conclusion.
“President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR, has shown the courage to champion and lead this conversation. We must now push this reform across the finish line,” he said. The Ogun governor declared that Akeredolu’s influence would continue to be felt in Nigeria’s evolving security architecture.
“Aketi may be gone in body, but his spirit walks among us. Heroes never truly die. Aketi lives on in every Amotekun officer on night patrol, every farmer returning safely, in the SWDC statute books, and in every clause of the upcoming National State Police Bill,” he said. In his remarks, Ondo State, Lucky Aiyedatiwa, said Akeredolu’s advocacy for State Police had now moved from a regional campaign to the centre of Nigeria’s national policy and constitutional conversation.
Aiyedatiwa, who was Akeredolu’s deputy before succeeding him as governor, said the late governor had regarded public office as an instrument of service rather than an ornament of status. He said Akeredolu’s career as Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice of Ondo State, President of the Nigerian Bar Association, Governor of Ondo State and Chairman of the Southwest Governors’ Forum was defined by “intellectual rigour, legal scholarship, courage and an unmistakable commitment to justice.
” According to him, the theme of the colloquium was particularly fitting because Akeredolu had demonstrated through Amotekun that communities closest to security challenges must have a meaningful role in protecting themselves.
“The establishment of the Southwest Security Network, the Amotekun Corps, represented a bold assertion that those closest to the people must have a meaningful role in protecting them,” Aiyedatiwa said. He noted that what Akeredolu and other Southwest leaders once advanced as a response to the realities of Nigeria’s federal structure had now become part of the country’s national policy discussion.
“What Akeredolu and other progressive voices once advanced as a necessary response to the realities of our federal structure has now entered the very centre of Nigeria’s national policy and constitutional conversation,” he said. Aiyedatiwa said the challenge before the country was now to develop a State Police system that would be responsive, professional and accountable while protecting citizens against abuse.
“The Nigerian federation must find the balance between national cohesion and local responsiveness; between federal authority and subnational capacity; between operational effectiveness and fundamental rights,” he said. He listed credible recruitment and vetting, professional training, sustainable funding, effective oversight, respect for human rights, clearly defined jurisdictions and safeguards against abuse as essential components of the proposed architecture. The Ondo governor said Akeredolu’s greatest lesson was that leadership required the courage to stand by convictions even when they were unpopular.
“He demonstrated that courage in public office is not the absence of opposition; it is the willingness to remain faithful to a conviction even when the wisdom of that conviction has not yet become universally apparent,” Aiyedatiwa said. He added that the most fitting memorial to Akeredolu would be “a Nigeria that is safer, more federal, more just and more institutionally responsive to its citizens.
” In his goodwill message, the former Ekiti State Governor, Dr Kayode Fayemi, paid tribute to Akeredolu, recalling the late governor’s courage, commitment to justice, and advocacy for a more decentralised security architecture. Fayemi, who worked closely with Akeredolu during their years in the Southwest Governors’ Forum, described his late colleague as a leader whose convictions were stronger than political convenience and whose contribution to the debate on multi-level policing had outlived his tenure in office.
He said Akeredolu’s contribution to the Southwest went beyond the creation of a security outfit, stressing that the late governor demonstrated how regional cooperation could provide practical solutions to challenges confronting individual states. Fayemi said Akeredolu’s legacy should therefore be measured not only by the offices he held but also by the institutions and ideas he helped establish and advance.
Also, in another goodwill message, the Director-General of the DAWN Commission, Dr Seye Oyeleye, said the colloquium represented an opportunity to move the conversation on State Police from commemoration to implementation. Oyeleye said the security debate was no longer about whether Nigeria should establish State Police but about how such a system could be funded, trained, equipped, regulated and protected against political abuse.
“The debate on state policing is no longer about whether. It is about how. How do we fund it? How do we train and equip it?
How do we guard against abuse? How do we keep it accountable to the people, not to politicians? ” he said. The DAWN Commission DG said the issue was not a regional or ethnic agenda but a national imperative arising from Nigeria’s federal structure and security realities.
“This is not a regional agenda. It is not a Yoruba agenda. It is a national agenda. State Policing goes to the heart of our nationhood,” Oyeleye said.
